questions.stem: In the sentence "Stop beating about the bush and tell us what happened", the expression *beating about the bush* means
questions.explanation: To beat about the bush is to talk round a subject instead of coming to the point. The command *tell us what happened* that follows in the sentence confirms the sense: the speaker wants directness.

distractorRationale.b: A literal reading of the image, which is exactly what an idiom does not mean
distractorRationale.d: Confuses the expression with idioms of effort such as *put one's back into it*

questions.stem: In the sentence "He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party", the expression *let the cat out of the bag* means
questions.explanation: To let the cat out of the bag is to disclose something that was meant to stay hidden. The phrase *about the surprise party* shows there was information intended to be kept quiet.

distractorRationale.a: This is closer to *stirring up a hornet's nest* or *muddying the waters*
distractorRationale.c: Escape is expressed by idioms such as *off the hook*
distractorRationale.d: Costly error is expressed by idioms such as *pay through the nose*

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence in Standard English: "The management will ______ a decision at the next meeting."
questions.explanation: English fixes certain verb-and-noun partnerships, and *decision* pairs with *make*. We make a decision, make an effort and make a mistake, but we do homework, do business and do our best. There is no rule behind it; the partnership must simply be learned.

distractorRationale.a: *Do a decision* is a very common error, transferred from *do the work*
distractorRationale.c: *Take up* means to begin or to accept an offer, which is a different meaning
distractorRationale.d: *Give a decision* is used only of a judge or referee delivering a ruling

questions.stem: Choose the option that collocates naturally with the noun in this sentence: "______ rain kept the farmers indoors for two days."
questions.explanation: English says *heavy rain*, *strong wind*, *thick fog* and *high winds*. Each intensifier keeps company with particular nouns, so although *strong* and *heavy* both mean intense, only *heavy* partners with *rain*.

distractorRationale.a: *Strong* partners with wind, tea and coffee, not with rain
distractorRationale.c: *Thick* partners with fog, smoke and mud
distractorRationale.d: *Big* is used of size and is not an intensifier for weather nouns

questions.stem: In the sentence "After three days without power, the manager was at his wits' end", the expression *at his wits' end* means

options.text: completely at a loss about what to do next
no longer able to think clearly because of illness

questions.explanation: To be at one's wits' end is to have run out of ideas and be unable to see a way forward. Three days without power supplies the frustration that produces the state, but the idiom itself describes helplessness rather than anger.

distractorRationale.a: Anger may accompany the state, but the idiom names the loss of ideas, not the emotion
distractorRationale.c: The word *end* misleads readers into thinking of finishing a task
distractorRationale.d: The idiom has nothing to do with illness or mental health

questions.stem: In the sentence "The quarrel over the seating arrangement was a storm in a teacup", the expression *a storm in a teacup* means

options.text: a great deal of excitement about something unimportant
an argument among only a few people
a problem that grew steadily worse

questions.explanation: A storm in a teacup is a great fuss over a trivial matter — the storm is real but the container is tiny. A seating arrangement is exactly the sort of small matter the idiom is used to belittle.

distractorRationale.b: The idiom stresses triviality, not violence
distractorRationale.c: The number of people involved is not what the idiom comments on
distractorRationale.d: A worsening problem would be *snowballing*, the opposite of this image

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the idiom in its correct fixed form?

options.text: It was raining cat and dog when we set out.
It was raining cats and dogs when we set out.
It was raining cats and dog when we set out.
It was raining the cats and the dogs when we set out.

questions.explanation: An idiom is a fixed expression, so its wording cannot be altered even slightly. The established form is *raining cats and dogs*, with both nouns plural and no articles. Changing a single word makes the expression sound wrong to a fluent speaker, and examiners test exactly this.

distractorRationale.a: Both nouns have been made singular
distractorRationale.c: Only the second noun has been made singular
distractorRationale.d: Inserts definite articles that the fixed form does not contain

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "Chidi ______ his father in both looks and temperament."
questions.explanation: *Take after* means to resemble an older relative, which is precisely the meaning required. Phrasal verbs change meaning entirely with the particle, so the particle is not decoration but the heart of the expression.

distractorRationale.a: *Take up* means to begin an activity, as in *take up farming*
distractorRationale.c: *Take on* means to accept a responsibility or to employ somebody
distractorRationale.d: *Take over* means to assume control of something

questions.stem: In the sentence "After two failed appeals, the lawyer finally threw in the towel", the expression *threw in the towel* means

options.text: handed the case to a colleague

questions.explanation: The idiom comes from boxing, where a trainer throws a towel into the ring to stop the fight, so it means to admit defeat and stop trying. *After two failed appeals* supplies the exhaustion of options that leads to surrender.

distractorRationale.a: Changing tactics is the opposite of surrender; the idiom means he stopped altogether
distractorRationale.c: Losing one's temper would be *flying off the handle*
distractorRationale.d: Transferring a case is a specific action the idiom does not describe

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence in Standard British English: "The meeting was convened ______ very short notice."
questions.explanation: The fixed expression in the variety of English used in Nigerian examinations is *at short notice*. The preposition is part of the collocation and cannot be reasoned out from the meanings of the individual words, which is why these phrases must be learned whole.

distractorRationale.a: *In* is used with periods of time such as *in an hour*, not with this phrase
distractorRationale.c: *On short notice* is heard in American usage but is not the form expected here
distractorRationale.d: *By* would indicate a deadline rather than the shortness of the warning
